context: The height array is ht = [3, 8, 5, 2, 7, 7, 3, 4]. Initially i = 0 (shorter board, height 3) and j = 7 (taller board, height 4), giving a capacity of 21. The diagram keeps the shorter left board fixed and moves the pointer at the taller right board one step inward to show why this move cannot improve capacity.
description: The left pointer stays at i = 0 (height 3). The right pointer moves one position left from index 7 to j = 6 (height ht[6] = 3). Board 7 returns to gray to show that it is no longer selected. The light blue water rectangle narrows to span indices 0 through 6 at height 3. The label below reads “Moving inward from the taller board must reduce capacity” and gives cap = min(3, 3) × (6 - 0) = 18.

frames.explanation: The right height falls from 4 to 3, so the water level stays at min(3, 3) = 3. The width falls from 7 to 6, reducing the capacity from 21 to 18. The value 18 describes only this move from the taller board.
frames.title: Moving inward from the taller board

result: The same reasoning applies if we keep i = 0 and move j to any index from 1 through 6. The water cannot rise above 3, and the width is smaller, so none of these pairs improves on 21. The diagram shows only j = 6. The other cases follow from the same argument. The greedy search can rule out all these states with i = 0 and instead move the pointer at the shorter board.
summary: Keeping the shorter board in place and moving the other end inward reduces the width without raising the water limit, so capacity cannot increase.
title: Moving inward from the taller board
